mechanism: Work in L^2(-pi, pi), the square-integrable functions on the interval; f must be square-integrable for its coordinates and length to exist at all - that is the standing hypothesis on f. The inner product of f and g is the integral of f times g, the squared length of f is the integral of f squared, and f and g are perpendicular when that integral is zero. Everything here is for real-valued f, which is why the formula has no modulus bars; for complex f the inner product conjugates one factor and the squares become squared moduli. The sine functions e_n(x) = sin(nx)/sqrt(pi), n = 1, 2, 3, ..., are orthonormal. Orthonormality alone gives Bessel's inequality and nothing stronger: for EVERY f the sum of the squared coordinates is AT MOST the squared length. Equality is a separate question, and the quantifiers decide it. Two statements are true and they are different. Pointwise: for a given f, equality holds exactly when f lies in the closed span of the system. Universally: equality holds for EVERY f exactly when the system is complete, that is, an orthonormal basis whose span is dense. The card states the universal form, with 'for all f' written inside the left half of the biconditional. The naive pointwise reading 'equality iff complete' is false, and the sine system shows why: f = x (odd) already gives equality against the sines, 2*pi^3/3 on both sides, even though the sines are incomplete. Forward direction, cited: when the orthonormal system is complete, Bessel's inequality becomes the equality known as Parseval's identity. Converse direction, proved: if the system is not complete then, by the standard characterisation, there is a nonzero g orthogonal to every e_n; all of g's coordinates are then zero, so its coordinate sum is 0 while its squared length is positive, and equality fails for g. The two directions together give the universal biconditional. The sine system is the concrete instance: g = 1 is orthogonal to every sine, so the constant function alone certifies incompleteness, and equality fails for it (2*pi against 0), as it does for cos x (pi against 0) and x^2 (2*pi^5/5 against 0). The repair is to supply the missing directions. Adding the constant 1/sqrt(2*pi) AND the cosines cos(nx)/sqrt(pi) to the sines gives the trigonometric system, a complete orthonormal basis of L^2(-pi, pi) - a standard theorem; its span's density follows from the Stone-Weierstrass theorem (strictly, uniform density of trigonometric polynomials among continuous periodic functions, which then yields L^2 density by the usual steps). Note f = 1 is repaired by the CONSTANT direction, not by any cosine, so 'add the cosines' alone would not fix it; the constant term is essential. What the script does and does not do: it PROVES orthonormality symbolically and proves the converse instance; it ILLUSTRATES Bessel and Parseval on five witnesses of both parities; and it demonstrates that no finite witness set can establish completeness, by exhibiting a four-direction orthonormal system (Gram-Schmidt on {1, x, x^2, cos x}) that reproduces the exact squared length of all five witnesses yet is incomplete, its residual on cos 2x having positive norm. Completeness of the trigonometric basis therefore rests on the cited theorem, never on the witnesses.
title: Perpendicular isn't enough.
